steps.observation: Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The keeper of the Narrows Light, Eli Moran, lived alone on a wind-battered islet where the Atlantic funnelled its fury between two ragged headlands. The lighthouse, a spiral of salt-bleached stone, had stood there for 137 years, and for the last twenty Eli had wound its clocks, trimmed its wicks, and listened to the sea talk in its thousand dialects of wave and wind.

Each evening, at seven minutes past dusk, he climbed the 113 iron steps to the lantern room, carrying a can of lamp oil and a battered thermos of tea. He tended the great Fresnel lens the way a violinist polishes a Stradivarius, for he believed the light had a soul that responded to kindness. When the sun slipped under its quilt of horizon, he released the beam—pure, glass-cutting white—across waters stained indigo. The flash pattern was two longs, one short, a rhythm sailors called “the old man’s heartbeat.”

Though no ships had wrecked on the Narrows in decades, Eli kept watch as if the next one might appear at any moment, wounded and lost. He logged each vessel: 19:42, westbound cargo; 21:10, coastal trawler; 00:16, nothing but the constellation of a satellite skimming north. In the quiet hours between, he wrote letters he never mailed—to a brother long passed, to a girl he once loved, to his own future self.

One winter night, a blizzard erased the horizon. Snow spun like broken glass in the lantern’s glow, and the radio crackled with a mayday from the F/V Alma Rose: engine failure, adrift, six souls aboard. Eli’s pulse synced with the lens—two longs, one short—as he calculated bearings by memory. He telegraphed coordinates to the coast guard, then did the only further thing he could: he brightened the beam beyond regulation, feeding the lamp until the filaments sang, hoping the Alma Rose could steer by that single impossible star. Hours passed. Ice crusted his beard. He whispered, “Come on, girl, find the light.”

At 03:23, the radio hissed alive: “Narrows Light, this is Alma Rose. We have you in sight. God bless that lamp.” Eli leaned against the cold brass railing, relief thawing him from the inside out. He answered simply, “Steady as she goes.”

When dawn lifted the dark like a stage curtain, the Alma Rose rode safely in the lee of the island, coast guard cutter beside her. Eli looked down from the gallery and raised his thermos in salute. The captain shouted, “We wouldn’t be here without you!” Eli touched the warm lens as if patting the shoulder of an old friend. “Not without us,” he corrected softly.

Years later, automation came. Engineers installed sensors, motors, remote diagnostics. On Eli’s final evening, he climbed the spiral one last time. Tools were boxed, oil cans emptied, the clockwork stilled. Yet the lens, catching sunset’s last breath, flared crimson and gold, filling the room with the hush of cathedral glass.

Eli set a worn notebook on the railing, pages full of ship names, weather notes, unsent letters. He clicked a pen and wrote a last entry: “Light transferred to circuits. Heart remains.” Then he descended, stepped into a small launch, and motored toward shore. From the mainland road he looked back. The lighthouse beamed automatically: two longs, one short—the old man’s heartbeat, now beating without the old man. But Eli knew better. Somewhere inside the stone tower, every careful footstep, every night of waiting, every whispered “come on, girl” was still climbing those 113 steps.

And far out at sea, mariners who never heard his name would still see the flash and say, “That’s the Narrows Light. Steady as she goes.”
